latest_nl_proof:
We prove the three assertions in order.

First, Peak(t) has no consecutive integers. If m = 1, then Peak(t) = {1}, so this is immediate. Assume m >= 2 and suppose, for contradiction, that j and j+1 both belong to Peak(t) for some 1 <= j <= m-1.

- If j = 1, then 1 in Peak(t) gives t_1 = -1. Also 2 in Peak(t) forces t_1 = +1: if m = 2 this is the endpoint rule for m, and if m >= 3 this is the interior rule for 2. This is impossible.

- If 2 <= j <= m-1, then j is an interior index, so j in Peak(t) implies t_j = -1. On the other hand, j+1 in Peak(t) forces t_j = +1: if j+1 <= m-1 this is the interior rule for j+1, while if j+1 = m this is the endpoint rule for m. Again impossible.

Thus no two consecutive integers can both lie in Peak(t).

Now assume m >= 2.

We next prove that Peak(t) is exactly the set of odd integers in {1,...,m} if and only if t_i = (-1)^i for every i = 1,...,m-1.

Suppose first that t_i = (-1)^i for all i.

- Since t_1 = (-1)^1 = -1, the endpoint rule gives 1 in Peak(t).

- Let 2 <= j <= m-1. Then j in Peak(t) exactly when t_{j-1} = +1 and t_j = -1. Under the hypothesis, this is exactly when (-1)^{j-1} = +1 and (-1)^j = -1, which is exactly when j is odd.

- Also m in Peak(t) exactly when t_{m-1} = +1. Under the hypothesis this is exactly when (-1)^{m-1} = +1, i.e. when m-1 is even, i.e. when m is odd.

So Peak(t) consists exactly of the odd integers in {1,...,m}.

Conversely, suppose Peak(t) is exactly the set of odd integers in {1,...,m}. We show that t_i = (-1)^i for every i = 1,...,m-1.

Fix i with 1 <= i <= m-1.

- If i is odd:
  * If i = 1, then 1 in Peak(t), so t_1 = -1.
  * If i >= 3, then i is an odd integer with 2 <= i <= m-1, so i in Peak(t). By the interior rule, t_i = -1.
  Hence in all odd cases, t_i = -1 = (-1)^i.

- If i is even:
  * If i <= m-2, then i+1 is odd and 2 <= i+1 <= m-1, so i+1 in Peak(t). By the interior rule for i+1, we get t_i = +1.
  * If i = m-1, then m is odd, hence m in Peak(t). By the endpoint rule for m, t_{m-1} = +1.
  Hence in all even cases, t_i = +1 = (-1)^i.

Therefore t_i = (-1)^i for every i.

Finally we prove that Peak(t) is exactly the set of even integers in {1,...,m} if and only if t_i = (-1)^(i-1) for every i = 1,...,m-1.

Suppose first that t_i = (-1)^(i-1) for all i.

- Since t_1 = (-1)^0 = +1, the endpoint rule shows that 1 is not in Peak(t).

- Let 2 <= j <= m-1. Then j in Peak(t) exactly when t_{j-1} = +1 and t_j = -1. Under the hypothesis, this is exactly when (-1)^{j-2} = +1 and (-1)^{j-1} = -1, which is exactly when j is even.

- Also m in Peak(t) exactly when t_{m-1} = +1. Under the hypothesis this is exactly when (-1)^{m-2} = +1, i.e. when m-2 is even, i.e. when m is even.

So Peak(t) consists exactly of the even integers in {1,...,m}.

Conversely, suppose Peak(t) is exactly the set of even integers in {1,...,m}. We show that t_i = (-1)^(i-1) for every i = 1,...,m-1.

Fix i with 1 <= i <= m-1.

- If i is odd:
  * If i <= m-2, then i+1 is even and 2 <= i+1 <= m-1, so i+1 in Peak(t). By the interior rule for i+1, we get t_i = +1.
  * If i = m-1, then m is even, hence m in Peak(t). By the endpoint rule for m, t_{m-1} = +1.
  Hence in all odd cases, t_i = +1 = (-1)^(i-1).

- If i is even, then 2 <= i <= m-1 and i in Peak(t). By the interior rule, t_i = -1 = (-1)^(i-1).

Therefore t_i = (-1)^(i-1) for every i.

This proves all parts of the lemma.
role_in_parent: Shows that every sign sequence gives a nonadjacent admissible peak set, and converts the two extremal parity peak sets back into the two alternating sign sequences.
statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 1, and let t = (t_1,...,t_{m-1}) be a sign sequence with each t_i in {+1,-1}; when m = 1 this sequence is empty. Define Peak(t) subseteq {1,...,m} by: if m = 1 then Peak(t) = {1}; if m >= 2 then 1 belongs to Peak(t) exactly when t_1 = -1, m belongs to Peak(t) exactly when t_{m-1} = +1, and for each integer j with 2 <= j <= m-1, j belongs to Peak(t) exactly when t_{j-1} = +1 and t_j = -1. Then Peak(t) contains no two consecutive integers. If m >= 2, then Peak(t) is exactly the set of odd integers in {1,...,m} if and only if t_i = (-1)^i for every i, and Peak(t) is exactly the set of even integers in {1,...,m} if and only if t_i = (-1)^(i-1) for every i.

domain_restrictions: m is an integer and m is at least 1.
t has exactly m minus 1 entries.
Each entry t sub i is either plus one or minus one.
When m equals 1, the sequence t is empty.
The definition of Peak of t for the nontrivial case only applies when m is at least 2.
The index j in the peak membership rule ranges over integers between 2 and m minus 1.
The index i in the final sign pattern characterizations ranges over integers between 1 and m minus 1.
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every positive integer m and every sign sequence t of length m minus 1, the set Peak of t defined by the endpoint and adjacent sign rules has no consecutive integers. When m is at least 2, Peak of t is the set of odd positions in 1 through m exactly when the signs alternate minus one, plus one, minus one, and so on starting with minus one, and Peak of t is the set of even positions in 1 through m exactly when the signs alternate plus one, minus one, plus one, and so on starting with plus one.
quantifier_order: For every integer m with m at least 1.
For every sign sequence t of length m minus 1, with each entry equal to plus one or minus one.
Define Peak of t by cases depending on whether m equals 1 or m is at least 2.

If m is at least 2, for each integer j with 2 at most j at most m minus 1, membership of j in Peak of t is determined by the adjacent signs t sub j minus 1 and t sub j, with the endpoints handled separately.
If m is at least 2, for every index i from 1 to m minus 1, the odd peak characterization uses the condition t sub i equals minus one to the i.
If m is at least 2, for every index i from 1 to m minus 1, the even peak characterization uses the condition t sub i equals minus one to the i minus 1.

variables.domain: sequence of length m minus 1 with entries each equal to plus one or minus one; empty when m equals 1
variables.name: t

variables.domain: subset of the integers from 1 to m
variables.name: Peak(t)

variables.domain: integers with 2 at most j at most m minus 1
variables.name: j
variables.role: bound index in the membership definition of Peak(t)

variables.name: i
variables.role: bound index in the alternating sign characterizations

witness_dependencies: No existential witnesses are involved; all conditions are universal or definitional.
The parity characterizations depend on the entire family of equalities for all indices i from 1 to m minus 1.
The set Peak of t is determined uniquely by m and t once the sign sequence is fixed.
